Fintech · Product Positioning · GTM · User Acquisition
An independent acquisition strategy for Fold Money

The opportunity

Fold Money is an Indian personal finance management (PFM) platform built on the Account Aggregator ecosystem. It consolidates financial data across accounts and automates expense tracking, giving users a unified view of their finances.

A tweet from Fold in March 2025 sent me down a rabbit hole. The product was interesting, but what caught my attention was the acquisition challenge behind it.

India's open-finance infrastructure was expanding, but consumers still needed to understand the value of consent-based financial data sharing.

A 2024 CGAP–Sahamati survey found that over 25% of surveyed smartphone users had used consent-based sharing with PFM applications. Awareness of Account Aggregators, however, remained limited outside certain financial use cases.

My hypothesis: Fold's acquisition opportunity wasn't simply selling better financial tracking. It was making the value of automated financial visibility obvious before asking users to connect their accounts.

After all, a product designed to simplify your finances shouldn't require a finance lesson just to understand why you need it.

Everything Folds was my proposed approach to that challenge.

Project disclosure: This is an independent, unsolicited concept inspired by a Fold Money tweet. I was not affiliated with the company. None of the proposed campaigns were commissioned, executed or tested. The market evidence referenced here supplements the original creative proposal.

01 / Positioning: Lead with the job to be done

Fold addresses a familiar problem: financial information distributed across different services, requiring effort to consolidate and interpret.

Its functional differentiation lies in automated aggregation and transaction visibility.

I translated that into a benefit-led proposition: one place for the information, less effort to make sense of it.

The creative hypothesis was that reducing perceived effort would be a more immediate acquisition hook than explaining the underlying technology.

The infrastructure might be sophisticated. The first interaction with the product shouldn't have to be.

02 / Audience strategy: Find the adoption opportunity

I prioritised digitally native working professionals aged 22–35 as an initial audience hypothesis, based on their likely familiarity with digital payments and multiple financial services.

The objective was to reach consumers who already had relevant financial behaviours but hadn't necessarily adopted a dedicated PFM product.

The proposed acquisition journey had three jobs: establish problem recognition, communicate differentiated value and build confidence to try the product.

The figures in the pitch were proposed targets, not results.

03 / Creator-led acquisition: Reach beyond finance enthusiasts

Finance doesn't exist independently of everyday life. It influences spending, travel, food, shopping and practically every routine we have.

Which is why I found lifestyle creators a more interesting starting point than another round of finance explainers.

The Daily Fold explored lifestyle creators as a discovery channel for users who wouldn't ordinarily engage with personal finance content.

Spending diaries, everyday routines and purchasing decisions provided natural contexts for demonstrating Fold's use case.

The hypothesis was that familiar situations could create stronger initial relevance than finance-specific messaging alone.

I'd validate the channel through qualified traffic, install conversion and activation before committing to scale.

04 / Product-led storytelling: Demonstrate the outcome

The advertising system visualised fragmented financial information folding into one organised view.

This was a deliberate creative translation of the product's core utility: consolidation without the manual effort.

Rather than lead with integrations or technical architecture, the concept demonstrates the outcome a user receives.

The intended role was to improve value-proposition comprehension and motivate product exploration.

Sometimes the clearest product demonstration is the one that barely needs explaining.

05 / Experiential acquisition: Make the message memorable

The newspaper concept translated the same proposition into a physical interaction.

The reader folds a chaotic advertisement to reveal a simplified message.

I liked the idea of making the audience do the very thing the brand promised. The fold itself becomes the pitch.

I saw this primarily as a brand-recall opportunity, with the potential to drive measurable digital discovery through a dedicated landing page or trackable QR code.

It wasn't intended to replace performance acquisition; it would extend the central positioning into a different context.

06 / Community: Address the trust barrier

Financial-data access introduces a different conversion challenge from conventional consumer applications.

Users need to understand what they're consenting to, what information is accessed and how they retain control.

I proposed transparent participation in relevant Reddit communities, prioritising product education and useful responses over promotional acquisition.

The channel's role would be to support informed consideration and help reduce uncertainty around account linking.

Trust isn't something a clever campaign can manufacture. But a thoughtful acquisition strategy should know where it needs to be earned.

07 / Video: Make the product benefit immediate

The film takes the emotional cost of fragmented financial management and turns it into a simple product demonstration.

An overwhelmed person sits behind a mountain of bills, receipts and notifications. Their therapist suggests, “Let's unpack this.”

A third person enters, clears everything into a single phone displaying Fold and replies, “Let's not.”

The execution connects the emotional problem with the functional benefit.

The product isn't the joke. The unnecessary effort is.

How I'd measure the strategy

The proposed funnel was:

Relevant discovery → Product consideration → App installation → Account-linking activation → Repeat usage

I'd evaluate the work through channel-level install conversion, account-linking completion, time to first useful financial insight and D7/D30 retention.

The central question wouldn't be which creative generated the most attention. It would be which message brought in users who understood Fold's value well enough to activate and return.

These are proposed success measures; the campaign has no actual performance data.

The takeaway

Everything Folds was an exercise in connecting an emerging fintech capability with a recognisable consumer need.

The strategic challenge was translating account aggregation and automated financial tracking into a proposition that could support discovery, understanding, trust and adoption.

The creative system was how I proposed taking that positioning to market.

Good technology deserves more than a feature list. I wanted to see how far a simple, memorable idea could take it.

Selected Work · GTM Strategy · Market Localisation · Audience Research · Integrated Campaigns
The Sony Pictures India story, from the other side of the screen.

A Hollywood film might spend two hours in cinemas. Its India-market launch could occupy our desks for months.

At Surfing Monkey, Sony Pictures India was my primary account for nearly three years. As the agency's social and digital strategy lead and primary point of contact, I worked across 30+ Hollywood theatrical campaigns, from early launch planning to opening-weekend execution.

The work began three to four months before the first teaser.

Alongside agency leadership, I developed film-specific launch strategies covering audience segmentation, market opportunities, channel planning, partnerships, promotional concepts and campaign timelines.

And with a slate spanning action, animation, horror, comedy and everything in between, there wasn't exactly a universal playbook.

30+ Campaigns. One very busy operation.

30+ theatrical campaigns · ~20% reported engagement growth · 50M+ cumulative campaign views, impressions and engagement indicators

Each release required its own approach to the Indian market.

The starting point was understanding the film's intended audience, existing franchise equity, local cultural relevance and the communities most likely to engage with it.

That meant researching creators, entertainment pages, regional audiences, fandoms and niche communities across India — looking beyond follower counts to assess audience relevance and partnership fit.

A campaign targeting a particular region, demographic or interest group needed a different creator mix and messaging approach from one built around a mainstream franchise.

Those insights fed into the launch strategy documents I developed with leadership, spanning influencer collaborations, digital advertising concepts, contests, on-ground activations, content pillars and distribution plans.

The job was to translate a global entertainment property into a locally relevant campaign strategy, then help bring that strategy to market.

One Film. Ten Languages. A Rather Complicated Launch.

Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse was the most operationally demanding campaign of my Sony tenure.

The film's India release spanned 10 languages, multiplying the requirements around asset localisation, creative production, approvals, scheduling and publishing.

The agency's creative teams were producing adaptations at speed, while I coordinated between Sony, our internal teams and campaign partners to keep the rollout aligned.

A single teaser or trailer moment could mean managing numerous regional-language assets across Instagram, Facebook, YouTube and supporting promotional touchpoints.

And the work was happening simultaneously across multiple launch moments, not as a neat sequence of individual posts.

The campaign also presented substantial opportunities for local relevance, particularly through Pavitr Prabhakar and the collaboration with cricketer Shubman Gill.

My contribution covered the campaign's social strategy and execution, partnership research, scripts and copy, creative coordination and multi-platform rollout.

The film went on to become India's highest-grossing animated film at the time, in 2023. That achievement belonged to the broader film, studio and distribution ecosystem.

My role was to deliver a substantial part of its India-market digital campaign, ensuring that the global IP translated effectively across local audiences and platforms.

From Strategy Deck to Release Day

Across the Sony account, my responsibilities connected the entire social and digital campaign lifecycle.

Upstream strategy: Developing launch proposals with leadership, mapping audiences, researching regional opportunities, evaluating creators and shaping campaign concepts months ahead of release.

Campaign development: Translating strategy into creative briefs, content plans, collaboration proposals, scripts, ad concepts, contests and on-ground activation ideas.

Channel ownership: Managing Sony's Instagram and Facebook presence, developing YouTube-specific approaches and overseeing time-sensitive teaser, trailer and promotional rollouts.

Cross-functional delivery: Serving as the primary coordination point between Sony stakeholders, internal creatives, production teams and external partners — from initial plans through final approvals and execution.

Some initiatives were developed independently; others involved close collaboration with agency leadership and the wider team. The consistent responsibility was keeping the strategy and its execution connected.

What the Work Added Up To

Across the account, our campaigns generated a reported 50M+ in cumulative views, impressions and engagement indicators, alongside approximately 20% growth in engagement during my tenure.

Those are account-level indicators across multiple releases and platforms, rather than results attributable to one film or a single intervention.

The larger experience was in repeatedly taking global properties into a complex local market, building audience-specific launch strategies and coordinating their execution at scale.

Thirty-plus releases taught me that even when the product is already made, there's an enormous amount of strategy in deciding who it's for, what makes it relevant and how you get an entire market to pay attention.

And yes, a perfectly timed midnight trailer launch still feels rather satisfying.

0→1 Product Development · Market Intelligence · Positioning · GTM
From a two-word brief to a commercially launched product category.

The brief from leadership was simple: water lilies.

What followed was the product marketing work behind Monet's Echo: a new hand-cast aluminium furniture category developed at House of Creatomy.

Starting with Claude Monet as a creative reference, I mapped the competitive landscape, researched product forms and examined an opportunity at the intersection of two premium audiences: luxury furniture buyers and art collectors.

The hypothesis: build a differentiated product category for a niche within an already niche market.

Our internal research estimated a serviceable market of approximately ₹250 crore.

But first, the film.

Concept, script, creative direction and edit supervision by me, working with the production team.

From market intelligence to product definition

Research across competitors, hundreds of design references and Monet's paintings became a consolidated product direction presented to leadership.

Working with product designers, those findings informed the collection's development. Each finished piece could be traced back to a specific painting.

This was product strategy from the earliest stage: identifying the audience, developing differentiation and helping define what we would actually bring to market.

Building the route to market

The product marketing ownership continued through launch.

Collection naming, product positioning, messaging architecture, sales pitches, battlecards and catalogues established how the new category would be communicated and sold.

The GTM rollout brought that positioning to life through product photography, the documentary, digital campaigns and physical displays, culminating in the collection's first showcase at RAW Collaborative.

The market responded

The collection generated interest from the audiences it was designed to reach.

International enquiries through Adorno extended its discovery beyond India.

Architect Husna Rehman featured pieces from the collection in her videos and subsequently became a Creatomy customer, adding a prominent professional relationship to the company's architect network.

These were valuable early signals of audience relevance and opportunities for further business, rather than proof of product-market fit.

The outcome

A starting reference became a market-backed product proposition, a finished furniture category and a coordinated commercial launch.

My ownership ran from market opportunity and customer segmentation through product development, positioning, GTM and sales enablement.

And somewhere in the middle, a few paintings became furniture.
